accuracy.evidence: Checked against NASA ISS Facts and Figures (orbit about 400 km, about 16 orbits a day, crewed continuously since 2 November 2000, typical six-month stays), NASA 'Exercising in Space' (about 2 hours a day against bone and muscle loss), NASA food and sleep pages (drink pouches, sleeping bags fixed to the wall, tortillas because crumbs float), NASA Apollo 11 overview (20 July 1969, Armstrong then Aldrin; 12 moonwalkers on Apollo 11-17, last in December 1972), the FAI 100 km line, airliner cruise height 10-12 km, and NASA's Moon fact sheet (1.62 against 9.81 m/s2, about 1/6, so the same take-off speed gives about 6 times the height since h = v^2/2g). The adult text states gravity at 400 km is about 90% of surface gravity, which matches g(r) = g0 (6371/6771)^2 = 0.885. Parameterised answers a+b, 2*a and 6*a are whole numbers at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented children's ideas about space (Sharp 1996 and Vosniadou on children's astronomy; NASA education notes on 'no gravity in space'): there is air in space (predict 1, sun hat and goggles traps, challenge 'air', p3), astronauts live on the Moon now (robot saying 1, m4, challenge 'moon'), nobody ever walked on the Moon (m3, challenge 'never'), planes and the station fly at similar heights (predict 2, 'Planes fly' stop with its own feedback, challenge 'high'), water behaves as on Earth (predict 3, cup option, challenge 'cup'), there is no gravity on the station (robot saying 5, m7, adult paragraph 3) and the Moon has no gravity (challenge 'grav', 100 times option).

lab_distinct.evidence: Every scene is about astronauts themselves: dressing a figure whose helmet, air backpack, gloves and boots appear as they are chosen while the sun hat and goggles are refused; dragging a rocket up a snapping ladder of real heights (0, 10, 100, 400 km); choosing the space way to drink, sleep, eat and keep fit; and two side-by-side jumps whose dashed height lines show 30 cm against 180 cm. flagsolscale (1029) is about planet sizes and distances and flagfreefall (895) about falling and orbits for older learners; neither has suits, the station's daily life or Moon jumps. The lab_distinct gate keeps flag_astro.js under 30% similar to every other lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds out by doing: a trap suit part gets the reason it fails (no air), the rocket's wrong stops say what is there and which way to go (planes at 10 km are still in the air), each space-life choice is followed by why the Earth way fails where things float, and the two jumps draw height lines before the child chooses 2, 6 or 100 times, so the 1/6 pull is seen as a measured 30 cm against 180 cm. The step messages only confirm what the child just saw.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the scene then disproves: breathe in space without a helmet (yes, there is air up there), planes or the space station higher (about the same height), let go of water on the station (it falls to the floor), and where the astronaut jumps higher (on Earth). The completion message names the child's own prediction against the result.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating challenge questions with two tagged wrong answers each. why() gives seven distinct messages: air (no air, the helmet and backpack carry it), moon (no one lives on the Moon or the Sun), never (Armstrong in 1969, 12 people by 1972), cup (water floats out, use a pouch), high (10 km against 400 km, about 40 times), fit (floating weakens bones and muscles, 2 hours a day) and grav (the Moon pulls about 6 times less, not zero). Each names the slip and states the fact.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (rocket, helmet, float, pouch, straw, strong) and pass the kid readability limit; the adult text was cut into shorter sentences to pass the adult limit while keeping orbit, gravity and Apollo terms. Canvas labels shrink to fit at 360 px and every tile label is dark text on white or pale green.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph carries one idea: what an astronaut is and how high space is, why the suit is needed, life on the station, and the Moon landing with the jump. The adult text gives the key words, the NASA facts with numbers, three named mistakes with the gravity correction, and what the lab asks. The content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark and 360 px Android light screenshots part-way through each Show me: the suit tiles fill a 2 x 3 grid beside the astronaut with 13 px bold labels, the height ladder labels sit right of the rocket without clipping, the space-life choices are two 90 px keys, and after a layout fix the jump question moved to the top so the Jump keys and 2/6/100 times keys no longer overlap. Buttons use the young 56 px size.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: each suit part ('Put on: Helmet'), Up, Down and Stop here for the rocket, both space-life options named with the job, Jump on Earth, Jump on the Moon and the three 'times as high' answers, and Right or Slip. Each result is spoken through c.say and the canvas aria-label, challenge feedback sits in a polite live region, and right or wrong is always stated in words as well as colour. The walk gate's axe run was clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
